name: Black Rot
summary: Black rot is a fungus disease of apple that causes purple frogeye spots on leaves, a firm black rot on fruit, and sunken cankers on branches. Dead wood and old fruit on the tree carry it from year to year.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that grow bigger, with a brown or tan centre and a purple edge, like a frog's eye.
Fruit rot usually starts at the blossom end as a brown spot, then forms brown and black rings while the flesh stays firm and leathery.
Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard black mummy that can hang on the tree for a year or more.
Reddish-brown, sunken patches on bark that grow into cankers (dead areas) on limbs and branches, with twig dieback.
causes: A fungus (Botryosphaeria obtusa, also called Diplodia seriata) that survives on cankers, dead bark, dead twigs and mummified fruit.
Spores are spread by rain splash, wind and insects, mainly around petal fall, and enter leaves, fruit and wounds.
Warm, wet weather, wounds from hail, insects or pruning, and stressed or winter-injured trees favour it. Wood killed by fire blight is an easy entry point.

actions.text: Prune out cankers and dead wood, cutting well below the diseased area, and destroy the prunings by burying or burning them.
Pick up and remove all mummified fruit from the trees and from the orchard floor.
Remove shoots killed by fire blight, since the black rot fungus can live in them during the season.
Keep trees healthy with regular pruning and balanced feeding, and avoid wounding trunks, limbs and fruit.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Do yearly sanitation: remove dead wood, cankers and mummies before spring.
Keep trees vigorous and reduce stress, because weak trees get cankers more easily.
Limit wounds from tools, insects and hail where possible, because wounds are the main entry point.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if cankers keep spreading or many fruit rot despite sanitation.

sources.title: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot (Penn State Extension)
Black Rot and Frogeye Leaf Spot of Apple (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

name: Mosaic Virus
summary: Apple mosaic virus is a virus that causes pale or yellow patches on apple leaves, slows tree growth and lowers yield. It has no cure and spreads through infected planting material.
symptoms: Pale, cream or yellow spots and random patches of yellowing on leaves as they open in spring.
Slow tree growth and low fruit yield.
Severely infected trees can set far fewer buds.
Symptoms are stronger in some seasons, depending on spring temperatures.
causes: Apple mosaic virus, a virus living inside the leaves and shoots of the tree.
It spreads when buds or twigs from an infected tree are grafted or budded onto healthy trees.
Sources say insects and pollen do not spread it. Spread through natural root grafts is not considered important in orchards.

actions.text: Do not take buds or scion wood (twigs used for grafting) from infected trees.
Plant only virus-free, certified trees from a trusted nursery.
Mark trees showing mosaic and consider replacing badly affected ones with healthy stock, because there is no cure.
Ask your agriculture officer to confirm the problem, since leaf yellowing can also come from other causes.

prevention: Buy only certified virus-free planting material.
Use virus-free scion wood for all grafting and budding.
Keep infected trees out of any propagation block.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer to confirm the diagnosis and to find a source of virus-free trees.

sources.title: Apple Mosaic Virus (Utah State University Extension)
Apple mosaic virus (Extension Australia, Apple and Pear IPDM)

name: Rust
summary: Apple rust (cedar apple rust) is a fungus disease that makes yellow-orange spots on apple leaves and sometimes fruit. The fungus needs a second host, juniper or cedar trees, to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Small yellow spots on leaves in spring that grow into yellow-orange spots with a red border and tiny black dots in the centre.
Later in summer, small cup-like tufts form on the underside of the leaf, under each spot.
Raised orange spots on fruit, which may crack and turn brown; infected stems can cause early fruit drop.
On nearby juniper or cedar: brown galls (hard lumps) that grow orange, jelly-like horns in spring rain.
causes: A fungus (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) that lives on two hosts: juniper or cedar, and apple.
Spring rain swells the galls on juniper and wind carries spores to apple leaves and fruit.
Wet spring weather favours infection. Spores from apple leaves go back to juniper, not to other apple trees, so there is no spread from apple to apple.
In India this rust is not widely documented; the sources describe it from other countries.

actions.text: Look for galls on any juniper or cedar near the orchard and remove them before the orange horns form in spring.
Check young leaves in spring for yellow spots, especially in wet weather.
Prefer resistant apple varieties when planting or replacing trees.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant apple varieties that are resistant to rust.
Remove juniper and cedar trees near the orchard where practical; the closer they are, the worse the disease.
Scout every spring during wet weather, from tight cluster to a few weeks after petal fall.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if you see orange spots on leaves or fruit, to confirm what it is.

sources.title: Cedar Apple Rust (University of Illinois Extension)
Cedar Apple Rusts (NC State Extension Publications)

name: Scab
summary: Apple scab is a fungus disease that spots leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather. It can cause heavy losses and leaves fruit rough, cracked and unsellable.
symptoms: Young leaf spots are velvety, olive green to brown, with feathery edges that become sharper with age.
Badly infected young leaves thicken, curl, shrivel and drop.
Fruit spots start like leaf spots, then turn brown and corky; early infection causes cracked, uneven, misshapen fruit.
Late infection can show only in storage as small rough black spots.
causes: A fungus (Venturia inaequalis) that survives winter mainly in fallen leaves and fruit on the orchard floor.
Spores are released around bud break and through spring, and need wet leaves or fruit to infect.
Rain splash and wind spread more spores from spots during the season. Cool, humid spring weather favours it.

actions.text: Rake up or chop fallen leaves and fruit in late autumn so they rot faster and release fewer spores next spring.
Check young leaves and fruit early in spring and keep scouting, to catch the disease before it spreads.
Prune each year so the canopy dries quickly and spray, if used, covers well.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where available.
Choose a well-aired site and give trees enough spacing.
Prune every year to open the canopy and shorten the time leaves stay wet.
Do leaf-litter clean-up every autumn.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer for spray timing advice during wet spring weather.

sources.title: Apple Scab (eXtension Apples)

name: Leaf Spot
summary: Cherry leaf spot is a fungus disease that makes purple-brown spots and small holes in leaves. Badly hit trees lose leaves early, become weaker and give less fruit the next year.
symptoms: Purple spots on the upper side of older leaves in early summer, turning reddish-brown then brown.
Nearby spots join into larger dead patches with yellow around them.
Dead tissue falls out and leaves small holes, called a shothole look.
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and drop early; spots can also appear on leaf or fruit stalks.
causes: A fungus (Blumeriella jaapii) that survives winter inside fallen infected leaves.
In spring it releases spores that wind and splashing water carry to new leaves. Spores need wet leaves to infect.
Frequent rain in spring and early summer and mild temperatures make it spread fast. Plums can also be affected.

actions.text: Rake up and compost or remove fallen leaves in autumn to cut the spores available next spring.
Check leaves from early summer and act quickly if leaves are dropping early.
Keep trees healthy, since early leaf loss makes trees prone to winter injury and low fruit set.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Clean up fallen leaves every autumn.
Scout every year from early summer, because the disease returns where leaves were left.
Combine sanitation with any spray programme advised locally, as sprays work best that way.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if trees lose most of their leaves early in the season.

sources.title: Cherry leaf spot (University of Minnesota Extension)

name: Powdery Mildew
summary: Powdery mildew is a fungus disease that makes white powdery patches on the underside of young cherry leaves. Bad attacks distort leaves, cause early leaf fall and can mark the fruit.
symptoms: Small white powdery patches on the underside of young leaves, which are easy to miss at first.
Leaves can pucker, curl at the edges, turn brittle, bronze or die in spots, and fall early.
Sweet cherry fruit can become rough and russeted or get a dull whitish coating.
Fast, soft shoots and suckers are attacked first.
causes: A fungus that survives the winter as tiny fruiting bodies on fallen infected leaves and, to a lesser extent, in bark cracks.
In spring, rain or irrigation releases spores that blow onto young leaves. Spores from the white patches then cause new infections about every week.
Warm dry days with cool humid nights, crowded canopies, soft new growth and too much nitrogen fertiliser favour it. Old leaves resist infection.

actions.text: Check young leaves, especially on suckers and low spurs, from early in the season. Look at the underside of leaves in good light.
Thin out dense branches so air moves through the tree and leaves dry faster.
Cut off suckers in spring because their soft leaves are very easily infected.
Rake up and destroy fallen leaves late in the season, since the fungus overwinters on them.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser that pushes soft, lush growth.
Choose varieties that show some resistance where available; some sweet cherry types are much more susceptible than others.
Prune every year to keep the canopy open and the tree at a size you can reach and inspect.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if white powdery growth keeps returning or spreads to fruit.

sources.title: Cherry Powdery Mildew in Utah

name: Anthracnose
summary: Anthracnose of peach is a fungus rot of ripening fruit. It starts as small round sunken spots that stay firm, and in humid weather orange spore masses ooze out in rings.
symptoms: Small, round, sunken spots on fruit that stay firm as they grow, unlike brown rot.
In wet or humid weather, salmon or orange coloured spore masses ooze from the spots in rings.
Symptoms appear only when fruit is ripe or nearly ripe, even though infection happened much earlier.
causes: A Colletotrichum fungus. The fungus survives the winter on diseased fruit and infected twigs.
Infection happens soon after blossom time, but the rot shows only as fruit ripens.
Wet, humid weather brings out the spore masses and spreads the disease.

actions.text: Pick off and destroy infected fruit and cut out diseased twigs, and dispose of them away from the orchard.
Prune and thin the tree so air moves through and fruit and leaves dry quickly.
Do not leave fallen or rotten fruit under trees because they carry the fungus to the next season.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Prune, thin and space trees every year for good airflow.
Keep the orchard clean of old fruit and dead twigs.
Check fruit and twigs each season so you can tell this rot from brown rot early.
help: Ask your agriculture extension officer to confirm whether fruit spots are anthracnose or brown rot before you act.

sources.title: Anthracnose Fruit Rot of Peach (University of Kentucky Fruit Scout)

name: Brown Rot
summary: Brown rot is a fungus disease that kills peach blossoms and twigs and rots ripening fruit into dry, wrinkled mummies. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Blossoms turn brown, wither and die, often covered with a brownish-gray mass of spores.
Fruit gets soft brown spots that spread fast and bear tan, powdery spore masses.
Rotted fruit dries into a wrinkled mummy that often stays hanging on the tree.
Twigs can form cankers (dead sunken patches) with gum, and leaves on those twigs may brown and wither.
causes: A fungus (Monilinia fructicola) that survives the winter in mummified fruit on the ground or tree and in cankers from the last season.
Spores spread by wind, rain splash and insects. They need a film of water on the plant for at least 5 hours to infect.
Wounds from insects, hail, cracking or rough handling let the fungus in, and fruit touching each other pass it on. Wet weather with moderate temperatures favours it.

actions.text: Pick up and destroy dropped and rotted fruit, and remove mummies from the tree.
Prune out cankers and blighted twigs in the dormant season and destroy them by burning or deep burial.
Control insects that feed on fruit, and handle ripe fruit gently to avoid cuts and bruises.
Remove wild or neglected stone fruit trees nearby that harbour the fungus.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Keep the orchard floor and packing area free of rotten fruit.
Cool harvested fruit quickly and store it cold.
Choose varieties with better resistance when you can.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if blossoms or fruit rot every season despite sanitation.

sources.title: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)
Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)

name: Leaf Curl
summary: Peach leaf curl is a fungus disease that makes new leaves thick, twisted and reddish in spring. Badly hit leaves turn pale and fall, which weakens the tree.
symptoms: Reddish areas on young leaves in early spring that thicken, pucker and curl.
Thick areas turn pale yellow and then grayish white as spores form on them.
Affected leaves turn brown or yellow and may drop, so the tree loses vigour and fruit.
Young shoots can be stunted or twisted, and rarely fruit shows red, wrinkled, corky patches.
causes: The fungus Taphrina deformans. It survives on twigs, in bark cracks and around buds.
Wind and rain wash spores onto swelling buds and opening leaves in early spring.
Cool, wet weather with high humidity at bud swell and leaf opening favours infection. Warm weather with fast leaf growth rarely allows it.

actions.text: Note the trees and branches affected this year. Once leaves are curled, the damage for this season cannot be undone.
Help weakened trees by thinning fruit, watering during dry spells and feeding the tree sensibly.
Prune in the dormant season and remove fallen curled leaves to cut the spores that carry over.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant peach or nectarine varieties that tolerate leaf curl where available.
Keep trees vigorous with pruning, feeding and watering.
Plan protection before bud swell next season, not after leaves have curled, and ask your officer about timing.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer before bud swell to plan timing for next season, because curled leaves cannot be cured.

sources.title: Peach Leaf Curl (West Virginia University Extension)
Peach Leaf Curl and Plum Pocket (University of Illinois Extension)

name: Rust
summary: Peach rust is a fungus disease that causes bright yellow angular spots on the upper side of leaves and rusty brown spore masses underneath. It can cause early leaf fall and spotted fruit.
symptoms: Bright yellow, angular spots on the upper leaf surface.
Brown to reddish-brown spore masses on the underside of the leaf.
Early attacks can cause leaves to fall in mid-season.
Small brownish spots with green halos on fruit, which become sunken as the fruit ripens.
Small cankers (bark splits) on twigs in spring.
causes: The rust fungus Tranzschelia discolor. It survives the winter in twig lesions.
Spores from twigs infect leaves in spring, and leaf spores then infect fruit and twigs. Spores need wetness to infect.
Heavy or late rain, sprinkler or flood irrigation that wets leaves, and damp air from weeds or nearby water favour it. Fruit is most at risk when nearly full size.

actions.text: If you use sprinklers, aim them low or shield them so leaves are not wetted.
Check fruit every second week after colour starts to change, so you spot rust early.
Keep weeds and low vegetation under trees cut down so air stays drier around the tree.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Use drip irrigation instead of flood, furrow or sprinkler irrigation where you can.
Avoid planting in damp, low spots near standing water.
Keep the orchard floor weed free to reduce humidity.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaves fall early in mid-season or fruit spots appear.

sources.title: Peach Rust (UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines)
Rust of Peach and Prune (UC IPM)

name: Scab
summary: Peach scab is a fungus disease that makes olive-green to black velvety spots on fruit, twigs and leaves. The skin may crack, and bad attacks cause small, distorted fruit.
symptoms: Small round olive-green spots on fruit, mostly near the stem end on the sunny side, that can join into dark velvety blotches.
Severe attack can stunt or distort fruit, crack the skin and cause early fruit drop.
Small yellowish spots on leaves that can fall out and leave shot-holes, with early leaf drop in wet seasons.
Twig spots are slightly raised, round to oval and brown, and infected twigs can die back.
causes: A fungus (Cladosporium carpophilum) that survives the winter as spots on twigs infected the previous year.
Spores form on twig spots and are splashed or blown by rain and mist onto fruit and leaves from about shuck fall. Spots show 40 to 70 days later.
Wet spring and early summer weather, warm humid days, and low, shaded sites with poor airflow favour it.

actions.text: Cut out and destroy scabby twigs before spring growth starts.
Remove or destroy wild or neglected peach, plum and apricot trees nearby.
Prune to open the canopy so fruit and leaves dry faster after rain.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.
Lightly spotted fruit is only skin deep, and peeling makes it fit to eat or process.

prevention: Avoid planting in low, shaded spots with poor drainage and air movement.
Prune every year to keep air moving through the tree.
Keep nearby stone fruit trees clean of disease.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if scab spots appear on most of the fruit in your orchard.

sources.title: Peach Scab (Ohioline, Ohio State University)
Peach Scab (Northeast Tree Fruit)

name: Bacterial Spot
summary: Bacterial spot is a disease caused by bacteria that spots plum leaves, fruit and twigs. Leaves get angular spots and shot-holes, and fruit can pit, crack and become unmarketable.
symptoms: Angular yellowing or dead spots on leaves, often with yellow halos, whose centres fall out to leave a shot-hole look.
Severe attack makes leaves fall early.
Fruit gets purple-black flecks, pits, cracks and gum, and spotted fruit rots more easily.
Small gummy, water-soaked cankers on twigs in spring can girdle them and kill the tips.
causes: A bacterium, Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, that survives the winter in diseased twigs.
In spring it spreads from cankers by splashing rain and insects. Wind-blown sand and sprayer wind create small wounds that help it enter.
Rain, dew, high humidity and wet leaves favour infection. Fruit is most at risk from shuck split until pit hardening.

actions.text: Cut out gummy, blackened twig tips in spring pruning and destroy them to reduce the bacteria.
Rake up and destroy fallen leaves.
Prune to open the canopy for air circulation.
Check leaves in light from spring through mid-summer, especially near the main veins.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant varieties with better resistance, especially on sandy sites.
Put susceptible varieties inside the block and resistant ones on the exposed edge, and plant windbreak trees on the windward side.
Use sod strips between trees and control dust from nearby dirt roads.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if twig cankers or leaf spots keep returning each season.

sources.title: Bacterial spot of peach and plum (Michigan State University Extension)
Bacterial Spot of Stone Fruits (Oklahoma State University Extension)

name: Brown Rot
summary: Brown rot is a fungus disease that kills plum blossoms and twigs and rots ripening fruit into dry, wrinkled mummies. It is worst in warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Blossoms turn brown, wither and die, often covered with a brownish-gray mass of spores.
Fruit gets soft brown spots that spread fast and bear tan, powdery spore masses.
Rotted fruit dries into a wrinkled mummy that often stays hanging on the tree.
Twigs can form cankers (dead sunken patches) with gum, and leaves on those twigs may brown and wither.
causes: A fungus (Monilinia fructicola) that survives the winter in mummified fruit on the ground or tree and in cankers from the last season.
Spores spread by wind, rain splash and insects such as bees and beetles, and infect after a film of water has stayed on the plant for at least 5 hours.
Wounds from insects, hail or rough handling let the fungus in, and fruit touching each other pass it on. Symptoms are similar across stone fruits.

actions.text: Pick up and destroy dropped and rotted fruit, and remove mummies from the tree.
Prune out cankers in the dormant season and destroy them by burning or deep burial.
Control insects that feed on fruit and handle ripe fruit gently to avoid punctures and bruises.
Remove wild or neglected stone fruit trees nearby that harbour the fungus.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Keep the orchard floor and packing area free of rotten fruit.
Cool harvested fruit quickly after picking.
Choose varieties with better resistance when you can.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if blossoms or fruit rot every season despite sanitation.

sources.title: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (University of Nebraska Extension G1965)
Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Ohioline, Ohio State University)

name: Pocket Disease
summary: Plum pocket is a fungus disease in which a few plums swell to many times normal size, turn spongy and hollow, and have no stone. The tree itself is usually not harmed.
symptoms: A small blister forms on young fruit soon after flowering and quickly spreads over the whole plum.
The fruit swells to about ten times its normal size, feels spongy and gets covered with velvety gray spores.
Later the fruit dries out and turns black, and it is hollow in the centre when cut.
Leaves may thicken and curl, but this is uncommon. Usually only a few fruit on a tree are affected.
causes: The fungus Taphrina communis. Wind and rain carry spores to fruit as it develops.
The spores survive the winter on twigs and bud scales and infect again the following spring.
Cool, wet weather during bud break and early fruit growth favours infection.

actions.text: Remove infected plums from the tree before they are covered with spores.
Bury infected fruit in a compost pile or deep in the soil, away from the orchard.
Promote tree health with pruning, feeding and watering.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available.
Keep trees vigorous with good pruning, feeding and watering.
Remove fallen and mummified fruit before spring.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if many plums on your trees are affected year after year.

sources.title: Plum pockets (University of Minnesota Extension)
Peach Leaf Curl and Plum Pocket (University of Illinois Extension)

name: Pox Virus
summary: Plum pox (also called sharka) is a virus disease of plum and other stone fruit trees. It marks leaves and fruit and makes fruit drop early. It cannot be cured, so infected trees must be removed.
symptoms: Pale green spots, rings, lines or yellow veins on leaves, often seen only in early summer.
Plum fruit can show rings or blotches, become pocked and deformed with sunken rings, and drop early.
Red rings and spots on plum stones, visible when the fruit is cut open.
Some infected trees show no clear symptoms for up to 3 years, and symptoms may fade in hot weather.
causes: Plum Pox Virus, a virus spread over long distances by infected budwood, rootstocks and nursery plants, which may show no symptoms.
Within an orchard, winged aphids carry it from tree to tree. Suckers from infected rootstocks and root grafts can also carry it.
Many wild and ornamental Prunus trees can carry the virus and act as sources.

actions.text: Report any suspected infected tree to your agriculture officer without delay, because the virus cannot be cured and the tree must be tested.
Remove infected trees promptly, including roots and suckers, as advised by your officer.
Do not let aphids feed on trees waiting to be removed, since they can still spread the virus.
Dispose of cull fruit away from healthy orchards, and control weeds in and near the orchard.

prevention: Buy only virus-free, certified trees and budwood from trusted nurseries.
Do not move plant material from infected areas.
Do not rely on insecticides to stop the spread, because aphids can pass the virus quickly.
Check trees each season and test leaf samples, since looking alone misses infections.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer at once if you suspect plum pox, because infected trees can spread it to your whole orchard.

sources.title: Plum Pox: A New Threat to Stone Fruit Production in the United States (Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station)
Sharka (Plum Pox Virus) in stone fruit and ornamental Prunus species (Ontario)

name: Rust
summary: Plum rust is a fungus disease that makes yellow spots on the upper side of leaves and brown spore pustules on the underside. Bad attacks make leaves yellow and fall.
symptoms: Yellow spots on the upper leaf surface.
Brown spore pustules (small raised dots) on the underside of the leaf.
Infected leaves take a yellowish cast and may drop in large numbers.
Symptoms become more common toward the end of summer.
causes: Rust fungi (Tranzschelia discolor and Tranzschelia pruni-spinosae). Anemone plants are an alternate host for one of them.
The fungus survives the winter in twig lesions. Spores from twigs infect leaves in spring, and leaf spores then infect fruit and twigs.
Spread continues while leaves stay wet or the air is humid. Abundant or late rain and sprinkler irrigation that wets leaves favour it.

actions.text: Check leaves on the underside for brown pustules, especially late in the season.
Use drip irrigation, or aim sprinklers low or shield them so leaves are not wetted.
Cut down weeds and low plants under the trees to reduce humidity around the tree.
Ask your agriculture officer which registered spray is suitable for this crop, and follow the label exactly.

prevention: Prefer drip irrigation over flood, furrow or sprinkler irrigation.
Avoid damp, low spots near standing water for planting.
Keep the orchard floor weed free.
help: Contact your agriculture extension officer if leaves yellow and drop early in the season.

sources.title: Prune and Plum (Prunus spp.) - Rust (Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks)
Rust of Peach and Prune (UC IPM)
